hints: Terminal velocity is the constant value reached when the velocity–time curve becomes horizontal.
Read the y-value of the horizontal plateau near the right-hand side of the graph.
walkthrough: Terminal velocity is shown by the horizontal part of a velocity–time graph, because the velocity is then constant.
The curve levels at 39 m s⁻¹.
Therefore the skydiver's terminal velocity is 39 m s⁻¹.

ai_rubric.observable: States 39 m s⁻¹ as the terminal velocity.

hints: Instantaneous acceleration is the gradient of a tangent to the velocity–time curve at the stated time.
Draw a tangent at 9.0 s, choose two well-separated points on that tangent, and calculate change in velocity divided by change in time.
walkthrough: Draw a straight tangent to the curve at t = 9.0 s; a tangent gives the instantaneous gradient.
Choose two convenient points on the tangent, for example approximately (0 s, 26 m s⁻¹) and (18 s, 44 m s⁻¹).
The gradient is Δv / Δt = (44 − 26) / (18 − 0) = 1.0 m s⁻².
Therefore the acceleration at 9.0 s is about 1.0 m s⁻².

ai_rubric.observable: Draws a tangent to the velocity–time curve at 9.0 s.
Uses the tangent gradient to obtain an acceleration between 0.9 and 1.1 m s⁻².

hints: Take downward as positive, then compare the downward weight with the stated upward drag force.
Calculate the resultant force first, then divide it by 68 kg; interpret a negative answer using the chosen direction.
walkthrough: Take downwards as positive. The weight is W = mg = 68 × 9.81 = 667 N downwards.
The drag force is 1800 N upwards, so the resultant force is 667 − 1800 = −1133 N.
The negative sign means the acceleration is upwards, so its magnitude is 17 m s⁻² upwards.

ai_rubric.observable: Combines the 68 × 9.81 N weight with the 1800 N drag force to obtain a resultant force of about −1133 N when downwards is positive.
Uses resultant force divided by 68 kg to obtain an acceleration magnitude of about 17 m s⁻².
States that the acceleration is upwards.

hints: Between t2 and t3 the skydiver is still moving downward but slowing, so consider how drag depends on speed.
Link the reducing drag force to the resultant force and then to acceleration as she approaches her new constant speed.
walkthrough: From t2 to t3, the skydiver's downward speed decreases towards 5.7 m s⁻¹.
As her speed decreases, the upward drag force decreases.
Her weight is constant, so the resultant upward force decreases in magnitude.
By F = ma, the magnitude of the upward acceleration decreases and becomes zero when she reaches constant velocity at t3.

ai_rubric.observable: States that drag force decreases as the skydiver's speed decreases.
Explains that the resultant force, and therefore the magnitude of the acceleration, decreases to zero as constant velocity is reached.

hints: Use the 39 m s⁻¹ terminal velocity at t1 and the 5.7 m s⁻¹ constant velocity at t3 with Δp = m(v − u).
Choose one direction as positive and retain the sign of the velocity change.
walkthrough: Take downwards as positive. At t1, u = +39 m s⁻¹; at t3, v = +5.7 m s⁻¹.
The change in momentum is Δp = m(v − u) = 68(5.7 − 39).
Therefore Δp = −2264 N s, which rounds to −2300 N s.
The negative sign means that the momentum change is upwards; its magnitude is 2300 N s.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Δp = m(v − u), or an equivalent signed momentum-change relationship.
Uses 68 kg, 39 m s⁻¹ and 5.7 m s⁻¹ to obtain −2300 N s, or the equivalent 2300 N s upwards.
